goldens.comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).

The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.

adjudication_records.issue_text: OR branch in deleteMany drops the method: SMS filter, deleting reminders of every method and causing silent data loss of non-SMS scheduled reminders

adjudication.rationale: In deleteMany, the new `where: { OR: [...] }` has a second branch `{ retryCount: { gt: 1 } }` without `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS`. This means any `WorkflowReminder` record of any method with `retryCount > 1` will be deleted, not just SMS reminders. That is a real broadening of the delete condition and can cause unintended deletion of non-SMS reminders if their retryCount is incremented elsewhere (or in the future).

adjudication_records.issue_text: Retry-eligible reminders are deleted before the scheduling loop reads them, destroying un-sent reminders whose window is still open, with no log or operator-visible trace

adjudication.rationale: The diff does delete reminders with `retryCount > 1` at the very start of the handler (`deleteMany` with an `OR` that includes `{ retryCount: { gt: 1 } }`), before the later `findMany`/scheduling loop runs. This means any unsent reminder that has exceeded that retry threshold will be removed regardless of `scheduledDate` (no date constraint on that OR branch), with no logging around the deletion. However, whether those reminders are still “retry-eligible” is a policy decision not shown in the diff; the new logic may intentionally cap retries and delete after the cap. So it’s a concrete, diff-grounded operational concern (silent deletion), but not a verifiable correctness bug on its own.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Retry increment in the catch block can throw a second unhandled exception, aborting the whole batch loop and skipping every subsequent reminder

adjudication.rationale: In the new catch block, the code now does `await prisma.workflowReminder.update({ ... retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 })` without any nested try/catch (diff hunk around `} catch (error) { ... }`). If that update fails (e.g., DB error, record missing), it will throw from within the catch handler and propagate out of the per-reminder try/catch, aborting the loop and preventing subsequent reminders from being processed. This risk is introduced by the diff (previously catch only logged).

adjudication_records.issue_text: No tests anywhere in the diff for the new retry-count state machine, including deletion of retryCount=2 reminders, survival of retryCount<=1, non-SMS reminder protection, and retry persistence

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces nontrivial new retryCount behavior (schema/migration adds retryCount default 0; API now deletes reminders with retryCount > 1 via an OR in deleteMany; scheduling logic increments retryCount on failure paths), but the PR diff contains no corresponding test changes validating this new state machine (e.g., that only retryCount>1 are purged, retryCount<=1 survive, non-SMS reminders aren’t unintentionally deleted by the retryCount branch, and retryCount increments persist).

adjudication_records.issue_text: The select spread + manual cast duplicates the source of truth for retryCount's presence in the query result, risking silent NaN at runtime if the field is renamed or the cast becomes stale

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `select: { ...select, retryCount: true }` but then manually casts the result to `(PartialWorkflowReminder & { retryCount: number })[]`. This does duplicate the “source of truth” between the Prisma `select` and the asserted TypeScript type, which can mask future mismatches (e.g., if the query changes but the cast doesn’t). However, in this diff `retryCount` is explicitly selected, so the claimed runtime `NaN` risk isn’t currently verifiable as a defect from the shown code; it’s primarily a type-safety/maintainability concern.

adjudication_records.issue_text: deleteMany OR clause retryCount branch deletes reminders of ALL methods, not just SMS, because it lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter

adjudication.rationale: In `scheduleSMSReminders.ts`, the `deleteMany` filter was changed to `OR: [{ method: SMS, scheduledDate <= now }, { retryCount > 1 }]`. The second OR branch lacks `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS`, so it will delete *any* `WorkflowReminder` with `retryCount > 1` regardless of method or date, which contradicts the surrounding intent/comments and can cause unintended data loss for non-SMS reminders.

adjudication_records.issue_text: retryCount is incremented but no retry is ever attempted — no resend path, no cap on send side, no alerting; reminders failing twice are silently deleted

adjudication.rationale: The diff does introduce a retry counter (schema/migration) and increments it on scheduling failures (the new `else` branch and in `catch`). However, the only functional use of `retryCount` shown is the pre-pass `deleteMany` with `OR: [{ method: SMS, scheduledDate <= now }, { retryCount: { gt: 1 } }]`, which will delete any reminder after 2 failed attempts, regardless of scheduledDate/method, with no explicit logging/alerting tied to that deletion. While retries can still occur implicitly on subsequent runs (since the query for `unscheduledReminders` does not filter out `retryCount > 0`), the review concern that the retry mechanism is incomplete/ends in silent dropping after two failures is grounded in this diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: retryCount update in catch block is unguarded and can itself throw, aborting the loop and skipping remaining unscheduled reminders

adjudication.rationale: In the per-reminder `try { ... } catch (error) { ... }` block, the catch handler performs `await prisma.workflowReminder.update({ ... })` without its own guard. If that update throws (e.g., DB connectivity, record missing), the exception will escape the catch block and reject the handler, which would stop processing remaining reminders in the loop. This behavior is directly implied by the unguarded `await` inside `catch` in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: deleteMany OR clause drops the method filter for the retryCount branch, deleting WorkflowReminder rows of any method with retryCount > 1 and SMS rows with retryCount > 1 regardless of scheduledDate, with no cancelled/booking-state check

adjudication.rationale: In `prisma.workflowReminder.deleteMany`, the new `where: { OR: [...] }` has a second branch `{ retryCount: { gt: 1 } }` with no `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` constraint. As written, this will delete *any* `WorkflowReminder` row (regardless of method) once `retryCount > 1`, and will also delete SMS reminders with `retryCount > 1` even if `scheduledDate` is not past due. The diff shows no additional cancelled/booking-state predicates in this deletion query.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Retry increment uses read-modify-write (retryCount + 1 from fetched value) instead of atomic { increment: 1 }, causing lost updates under overlapping cron runs so the retry cap is never enforced and SMS can be double-sent

adjudication.rationale: The diff fetches `retryCount` in `unscheduledReminders` and then updates it via read-modify-write (`retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1`) in two places (the `else` branch after attempting to schedule and in the `catch`). Without an atomic DB-side increment (e.g. Prisma `{ increment: 1 }`), concurrent/overlapping executions that process the same `WorkflowReminder` can overwrite each other’s increments, leading to lost updates and making the new retry cap logic (`deleteMany` OR `retryCount > 1`) unreliable under overlap.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Catch-block retry-increment update is unguarded against P2025 when the reminder row was deleted between fetch and failure, escaping the try/catch, aborting the loop, and silently skipping remaining reminders

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `await prisma.workflowReminder.update({ where: { id: reminder.id }, data: { retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 } })` both in the `else` branch and inside the `catch` block. If the `WorkflowReminder` row is deleted after the initial `findMany` (e.g., by another process) and before this update runs, Prisma can throw (e.g., record-not-found/P2025). That thrown error is not wrapped in its own try/catch, so it would escape the surrounding `catch` block and abort the handler/loop, potentially skipping remaining reminders. This failure mode is introduced by the new update calls; previously the `catch` only logged.

adjudication_records.issue_text: deleteMany with retryCount > 1 branch permanently deletes future-dated reminders after two failed attempts, silently dropping reminders without cancellation event, cancelled flag, or log

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes the initial `deleteMany` filter to `OR: [{ method: SMS, scheduledDate <= now }, { retryCount: { gt: 1 } }]`, meaning any `WorkflowReminder` with `retryCount > 1` will be permanently deleted regardless of `scheduledDate` (including future-dated) and regardless of `method`. Since the code increments `retryCount` on both `!scheduledSMS` and in the `catch` block, a reminder can reach `2` and then be deleted on the next run without setting `cancelled`, emitting a cancellation event, or logging beyond the generic error log. This matches the finding about silently dropping reminders after two failed attempts.

adjudication_records.issue_text: New OR branch in deleteMany lacks method: WorkflowMethods.SMS guard, so any WorkflowReminder row with retryCount > 1 is deleted regardless of method, risking deletion of future reminders from other methods like email

adjudication.rationale: The updated `deleteMany` now uses `OR: [{ method: SMS && scheduledDate <= now }, { retryCount: { gt: 1 } }]`. The second branch has no `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` constraint, so it will delete any `WorkflowReminder` record (including non-SMS methods) once `retryCount > 1`. Since `retryCount` was added to the shared `WorkflowReminder` model (schema/migration), this can cause unintended deletion/data loss for other reminder methods.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Catch block's prisma.workflowReminder.update is unguarded; if it throws, the exception aborts the for loop leaving remaining reminders unscheduled this run

adjudication.rationale: In the `catch (error)` block, the code does `await prisma.workflowReminder.update(...)` without any additional guarding. If that update throws (e.g., transient DB error), the exception will propagate out of the catch and abort the current async loop/handler, preventing remaining `unscheduledReminders` from being processed in this run. This behavior is directly implied by the added `await prisma.workflowReminder.update` inside the catch.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Rows with retryCount = 2 and a successfully scheduled Twilio sid are deleted by deleteMany matching on retryCount alone, orphaning the Twilio send without audit trail and risking duplicate sends

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes `deleteMany` to delete any `WorkflowReminder` with `retryCount > 1` regardless of whether it was ultimately scheduled successfully (it’s in an `OR` with no other constraints). The scheduling logic increments `retryCount` on failure (`else` branch and `catch`), but on later success it only updates `referenceId: scheduledSMS.sid` and does not reset `retryCount`. Therefore a reminder can reach `retryCount = 2`, then later succeed and get a Twilio `sid`, and still be deleted on the next run purely due to `retryCount > 1`, losing the record/audit trail. This behavior is directly implied by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: OR branch deleting reminders on retryCount > 1 lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing EMAIL and other-method reminders with retryCount > 1 to be hard-deleted

adjudication.rationale: In `scheduleSMSReminders.ts`, the `deleteMany` filter was changed to an `OR` with a second branch `{ retryCount: { gt: 1 } }` that does not include `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS`. This will hard-delete *any* `WorkflowReminder` row (including EMAIL/other methods) whose `retryCount > 1`, which contradicts the comment/intent of deleting only scheduled SMS reminders and can cause unintended data loss.

adjudication_records.issue_text: OR branch lacks a past-scheduledDate constraint, so future-dated SMS rows reaching the retry path via the catch block get deleted

adjudication.rationale: The new `deleteMany` uses `OR: [{ method: SMS, scheduledDate <= now }, { retryCount: { gt: 1 } }]`, so any row with `retryCount > 1` will be deleted regardless of `scheduledDate` (and regardless of `method`). Since failures increment `retryCount` in both the `else` branch and the `catch`, a future-dated reminder (selected via `scheduledDate >= now` in the later query) can reach `retryCount > 1` after repeated failures and then be deleted on the next run even if its `scheduledDate` is still in the future.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Unscoped delete allows one booking's endpoint execution to delete another booking's reminder rows, creating cross-tenant data destruction

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows a global `prisma.workflowReminder.deleteMany({ where: { OR: [...] }})` with no tenant/booking scoping, but it does not show any per-booking endpoint context or multi-tenant constraints. The finding’s claim that “one booking’s endpoint execution” can delete “another booking’s” reminders is not verifiable from this diff alone (the handler appears to operate across all reminders).

adjudication_records.issue_text: deleteMany OR clause drops method and scheduledDate guards, causing retryCount>1 branch to hard-delete SMS and EMAIL reminders including future-dated and already-scheduled ones; scope should be AND: [{ method: SMS }, { OR: [...] }]

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes `deleteMany` to `where: { OR: [ { method: SMS, scheduledDate: { lte: now } }, { retryCount: { gt: 1 } } ] }`, which will delete *any* `WorkflowReminder` row with `retryCount > 1` regardless of `method` or `scheduledDate`. This drops the prior guards and can hard-delete non-SMS reminders (e.g., EMAIL) and/or future-dated reminders as the finding describes. The comment still claims it only deletes past-dated scheduled SMS reminders, so the broadened OR condition is likely unintended and risks data loss.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Retry exhaustion implemented by row deletion instead of state change, destroying audit trail; should set cancelled: true to preserve the record

adjudication.rationale: The diff implements retry exhaustion cleanup by deleting rows: prisma.workflowReminder.deleteMany now includes an OR branch `{ retryCount: { gt: 1 } }`, which will remove records once retries exceed 1. This does indeed destroy the record (and any audit/history) rather than preserving it via a state change such as setting `cancelled: true`. While this is a design/observability concern rather than a provable functional defect from the diff alone, it is a concrete, diff-grounded issue.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Catch-block retryCount increment runs even when exception is thrown after Twilio message was successfully sent, causing duplicate SMS scheduling and double-increment that accelerates the row into the destructive delete

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `retryCount` increments in the `catch` block (`workflowReminder.update(... retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1)`). If Twilio successfully sends (`scheduledSMS.sid` is obtained) but an exception occurs afterward (e.g., during the DB `update` that marks it scheduled), execution jumps to `catch`, increments `retryCount`, and the reminder remains unscheduled—so a later run can attempt to schedule again, potentially sending a duplicate SMS. Additionally, the new cleanup deletes rows where `retryCount > 1` (regardless of method/date), so repeated post-send errors can push a reminder into this destructive delete even though an SMS may already have been sent. The finding’s “double-increment” wording isn’t strictly shown (only one increment per run), but the core duplicate/incorrect retry escalation risk is grounded in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: OR retryCount > 1 delete branch lacks method: WorkflowMethods.SMS constraint, causing non-SMS reminders to be deleted
matched_golden_ids: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: The candidate flags that the OR branch for deleting when retryCount > 1 is missing a WorkflowMethods.SMS constraint, which leads to non-SMS reminders being deleted—this is the same underlying bug described in the golden comment.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Deleting at retryCount > 1 with increments in both else and catch branches means reminders are silently destroyed after two retries with no log or error

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a `deleteMany` condition `OR: [{ method: SMS & scheduledDate <= now }, { retryCount: { gt: 1 } }]`, so any `WorkflowReminder` with `retryCount > 1` will be deleted (even if not SMS, since the retryCount branch has no `method` constraint). The same diff increments `retryCount` on failures both in the `else` branch and in `catch`, but only the `catch` path logs; deletion itself has no logging. This makes it verifiable from the diff that reminders can be removed after reaching 2+ retries and that this can occur without any log in the `else` failure path.

adjudication_records.issue_text: else branch increments retryCount but still returns ok: true, falsely reporting success when SMS was never scheduled

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows an `else` that increments `retryCount` when `scheduledSMS` is falsy and also increments it in the `catch`, but it does not show any response being sent from that branch. The only visible `res.json({ ok: true })` is in the early-return when there are no `unscheduledReminders`. Any claim that the `else` branch "still returns ok: true" (and thus falsely reports success) is not directly supported by the shown diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: retryCount is consumed on possibly permanent failures (e.g., invalid phone number) then reminder silently deleted

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `retryCount` and increments it on scheduling failures (both in the `else` branch after attempting to schedule and in the `catch`). At the start of the handler it now deletes reminders with `retryCount > 1` via `deleteMany({ where: { OR: [..., { retryCount: { gt: 1 } }] } })`, regardless of method or scheduledDate. This means reminders that repeatedly fail (including potentially permanent failures like invalid numbers) will be dropped from the DB after a couple attempts, with no persisted failure state and (in the non-throwing `else` path) no logging—effectively silently deleted.

adjudication_records.issue_text: catch block swallows scheduling errors, increments retryCount, and reports ok: true during provider outages

adjudication.rationale: In the new logic, errors during scheduling are caught and not rethrown: the `catch (error)` block updates `retryCount` and only `console.log`s the error, then continues processing (`await prisma.workflowReminder.update({ data: { retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 }})`). Likewise, the non-success branch increments `retryCount` without surfacing an error. This can cause the API handler to complete normally even if the SMS provider is down, but the diff does not show the final `res.json(...)` path so the specific claim that it returns `{ ok: true }` during outages is not fully verifiable from the snippet.

adjudication_records.issue_text: no atomic/in-flight guard on retryCount increment allows concurrent cron invocations to double-send the same SMS

adjudication.rationale: The handler reads a batch of reminders via `findMany` (now selecting `retryCount`) and then sends SMS before updating the row. There is no transactional/conditional update (e.g., `updateMany` with a guard like `WHERE id=? AND referenceId IS NULL`) to claim the reminder, so two concurrent cron invocations can both select the same reminder and both send an SMS before either update lands. Additionally, the retry update uses `retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1` (not an atomic increment), which can lose updates under concurrency and keep a reminder retryable longer than intended.

adjudication_records.issue_text: concurrent runs read same retryCount and both write +1, consuming retry budget slower than actual send attempts

adjudication.rationale: The diff increments `retryCount` using a read-modify-write pattern (`retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1`) based on a previously fetched `reminder.retryCount` (see both update blocks). If two handler runs process the same reminder concurrently, they can both read the same value and each write back the same `+1`, losing one increment. This would undercount actual attempts and delay hitting the cleanup condition (`retryCount: { gt: 1 }`), matching the finding.

adjudication_records.issue_text: findMany has no retryCount filter, so retry cap correctness depends entirely on the earlier deleteMany side-effect

adjudication.rationale: In the diff, the `findMany` query does not include any `retryCount` condition in its `where` clause (it only adds `retryCount: true` to `select`). The only enforcement of a retry cap shown is the preceding `deleteMany` which deletes rows with `retryCount: { gt: 1 }`. So the retry-cap behavior is coupled to that earlier side-effect rather than being explicit in the `findMany` filter, which is a maintainability/clarity concern rather than a directly verifiable functional defect from the diff alone.
